Chapter 6: Deepening Collective Responsibility—Community, Relationships, and Shared Power
Now that we've built a foundation of self-awareness and personal accountability, it's time to look outward—toward the communities and relationships that shape our daily lives.
Antiracism isn't something you do alone. It's at its most powerful when you're connected with others. So, let's take a look at how we can move from individual change to collective responsibility—recognizing that real transformation happens not just inside us, but in the spaces between us.
Here’s something to pay attention to: white supremacy isn’t just upheld by individuals. It’s reinforced by groups—families, workplaces, schools, faith communities, and neighborhoods. These are the places where our norms are set, where behaviors are modeled, and where values get passed along.
If we want lasting change, we need to engage these communities—challenge old patterns, and start building new ones, together.
Think of it like a garden. Sure, you can tend your own little plot, but the health of the whole garden depends on everyone pitching in—pulling weeds, planting seeds, and sharing the harvest.
In the same way, antiracist work really flourishes when it’s rooted in shared effort and mutual support.
So, what are some practical ways to build this kind of collective responsibility?
First, you can initiate conversations. That means gently bringing up topics of race and equity in group settings—even when it feels uncomfortable.
Next, try modeling vulnerability. When you share your own reflections and even your mistakes, it opens the door for others to do the same.
Another key is building alliances. Connect with others who are committed to justice, and form supportive networks that hold everyone accountable.
And finally, focus on redistributing power. Actively seek out and amplify the voices of people of color in decision-making spaces.
Want some real-world examples? In a workplace, this could mean advocating for more inclusive hiring practices, or backing up colleagues who speak out about bias. In a family, it might look like talking openly with children about the history of racism, or gently challenging a relative who makes a harmful comment.
The key takeaway here is that change isn't usually quick or easy. Resistance is normal, and setbacks will happen. But what really matters is your willingness to stay engaged, to listen deeply, and to keep moving forward—together.
